newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-BOWE JOINS THE MARINES TO BE A KILLER.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-BOWE JOINS THE MARINES TO BE A KILLER.

text.p: Riddick Bowe, the former two-time heavyweight champion of the world, wants to be a killer.
Not a finisher in the ring when his opponent is hurt, which he has sometimes had trouble doing, but a full-fledged, card-carrying killer. He wants to be a Marine.
That's what Bowe said Thursday when he announced he has enlisted in the United States Marine Corps Reserves.
Yes, that's Marine Corps as in up in the morning at 4:30, spit-and-polish, drill sergeants screaming in your face all day, and in bed at 10:30 at night.

Why would a man who has earned about $100 million in and out of the ring, who has five children, a loving wife and a very comfortable life want to push his body further than many people even want to imagine?

"I need another challenge now. To have discipline, to finish boot camp, to take orders," said Bowe, who as a fighter has not always had the discipline to match his great ring talents, which were magnificently revealed at times, but at other times seemed squandered in battles with balooning weight and indifference.
"I'm going into the Marine Corps to be a killer," Bowe, 29, said at a news conference. "If war breaks out I'm going to war. If I gotta die defending my country, what a way to die."

Bowe, who will owe the Marines three years of active duty one weekend a month after Boot Camp, said he first wanted to join the Marines after high school but his wife, Judy, became pregnant so he dedicated himself instead to boxing.
Bowe, who earns millions of dollars for just one fight, will earn about $600.00 per month as a private in the Marines, said his manager Rock Newman said.

The multi-millionaire fighter, resplendently dressed in an expensive brown-green suit -- not far from the colour of a Marine uniform -- and a cream-coloured mock turtleneck shirt, said he would report on February 10 for eight weeks of Boot Camp training.

The affable, downright charming Bowe, who practiced saluting while wearing a Marine cap inscribed with words, "The Few, The Proud," said he will return to the ring. Newman, said the 40-1-1 Bowe likely will fight again late this year.
Bowe's last two fights were disasters.
He won both of them against Andrew Golota, but only when the Polish-born fighter was disqualified each time for low blows after thoroughly beating Bowe.
Golota inflicted terrible punishment on Bowe, at times battering him around the ring like a rag doll.
It seemed that based on those fights Bowe had reached the end of his career.
"It may enhance my boxing ability to eat the right food and give me more determination," Bowe said.

Bowe has been in several ring wars, most notably against Evander Holfield, whom he defeated in November, 1992 to win the undisputed world heavyweight championship, before losing it to him a year later.
It appeared Thursday that Bowe was slurring his words much more than he used to, raising concerns for his health.
The press release from the Marine Corps stressed that Bowe was "found mentally, morally and physically qualified" to go to the Marines' Boot Camp on Parris, Island, South Carolina, as a raw recruit.
But, of course, the effects of taking punches for a living often do not show up on tests to carry a rifle or do push ups.
Bowe, thoughtful and low-keyed, insisted he still had all of his faculties, but said, "I ain't stupid. I've been hit upside of the head, the whole nine yards. Eventually it's going to take its toll."

Bowe said his apparent slurring was because he "gets lazy" in his speech. Newman dismissed it, saying Bowe had slept on his private bus throughout the trip from the Washington, D.C. area and was still bleary-eyed when he met reporters.
Newman said he took Bowe to Parris Island to watch the recruits undergoing the rigours of training first hand, hoping his fighter would be dissuaded from joining up.
"I was kinda numb. I saw a guy getting this close," (he put his hand an inch in front of his face) spitting in his face," Bowe said.
Bowe, close to bragging about it, said he already can do more than the required number of "Marine style" pushups and pullups.
But there is a limit to what he will take in the Marine Corps, said Bowe, who is afraid of heights.
"I ain't jumping out of no planes."
